competent.prompt: A web server in a public subnet must serve HTTPS to the whole internet, but SSH must work only from the office range `203.0.113.0/24`. Which inbound security group rules do this?
options: TCP 443 and TCP 22 both from `203.0.113.0/24`
rubric: Open 443 to the world and restrict 22 to the office CIDR.
Other options swap the sources or open SSH to everyone, missing which port needs which scope.

competent.prompt: Versioning is enabled on an S3 bucket. You run `aws s3 rm s3://logs-bkt/app.log` without a version ID. What happens?
options: A delete marker is added and earlier versions remain
The latest version is deleted and the older one is promoted
All versions of the object are permanently deleted
The request fails until versioning is suspended
rubric: A plain delete on a versioned bucket adds a delete marker; old versions stay recoverable.
Distractors assume deletion is permanent or blocked.

competent.prompt: An application on an EC2 instance must read objects from one S3 bucket without storing any long-term credentials on the instance. What should you do?
options: Put an IAM user's access keys in `~/.aws/credentials`
Attach an IAM role with S3 read permission via an instance profile
Make the bucket public so no credentials are needed
Embed the root account keys in the application's config
rubric: Instance profiles supply temporary credentials automatically.
Stored keys or public buckets violate the no-long-term-credentials requirement.

competent.prompt: Instances in a private subnet need outbound internet access to download patches, but must not accept inbound connections from the internet. Which route table entry achieves this?
options: `0.0.0.0/0` to an internet gateway
`0.0.0.0/0` to a NAT gateway in a public subnet
`10.0.0.0/16` to a NAT gateway in the private subnet
`0.0.0.0/0` to a virtual private gateway
rubric: A NAT gateway in a public subnet gives outbound-only access.
Routing directly to an internet gateway makes the subnet public.

competent.prompt: You want to upload the local folder `./site` to `s3://my-bucket/site`, copying only new or changed files on repeat runs. Which command fits?
options: `aws s3 cp ./site s3://my-bucket/site`
`aws s3 mv ./site s3://my-bucket/site`
`aws s3 sync ./site s3://my-bucket/site`
`aws s3 ls ./site s3://my-bucket/site`
rubric: `sync` compares and copies only differences recursively.
`cp` without `--recursive` fails on folders and `mv` deletes the source.

competent.prompt: You must make a web tier behind an Application Load Balancer tolerate the loss of one Availability Zone. Which actions do this? Select all that apply.
options: Launch instances in subnets in at least two AZs
Enable ALB in subnets from at least two AZs
Place all instances in one larger instance type
Use an Auto Scaling group spanning both AZ subnets
rubric: Redundancy requires ALB nodes and instances in multiple AZs, ideally managed by an ASG.
A larger single instance remains a single point of failure.

competent.prompt: An Auto Scaling group has 4 instances and a target tracking policy of 50% average CPU. Traffic rises and average CPU reaches 75%. Max size is 10. Roughly what will the group do?
options: Scale out to about 6 instances to bring CPU near 50%
Scale in to 2 instances to cut cost
Do nothing until CPU exceeds 90%
Scale out immediately to the maximum of 10
rubric: Target tracking scales proportionally: 4 x 75/50 = 6.
Others misunderstand direction or ignore proportional scaling.

competent.prompt: An EC2 instance in a new subnet has a public IP and a security group allowing SSH, yet connections time out. The VPC has an internet gateway. Which cause is most likely?
options: The subnet's route table lacks a `0.0.0.0/0` route to the internet gateway
The security group needs an outbound rule for port 22
The internet gateway must be attached to the instance
The instance needs an IAM role for SSH
rubric: A subnet is public only if its route table sends internet traffic to the IGW.
Security groups are stateful so replies need no outbound rule; IAM doesn't govern network SSH.

competent.prompt: A Lambda function in private subnets of a VPC times out when calling DynamoDB, but works when not attached to a VPC. The subnets have no NAT gateway. What is the best diagnosis?
options: Lambda cannot call DynamoDB from any VPC
The function has no network path to DynamoDB's public endpoint
DynamoDB tables must be in the same subnet
The execution role lacks permission, which causes timeouts
rubric: VPC-attached Lambda needs a NAT or a gateway VPC endpoint to reach DynamoDB.
Missing IAM permission yields an AccessDenied error, not a timeout.

competent.prompt: A user's IAM policy allows `s3:*` on a bucket. The bucket policy has an explicit Deny for requests not coming from a specific VPC endpoint. The user calls from a laptop. What is the result?
options: Allowed, because the identity policy grants `s3:*`
Allowed, because the user is in the same account
Denied, because an explicit deny overrides any allow
Denied, because bucket policies always override identity policies
rubric: An explicit deny always wins in policy evaluation.
The last option overstates it: bucket policies only win here because of the explicit deny.

competent.prompt: A team moves 2 TB of objects read daily into S3 Standard-IA to save money, and the bill rises. What best explains this?
options: Standard-IA has higher storage rates than Standard
Standard-IA charges per-GB retrieval fees that outweigh storage savings for frequent reads
Standard-IA objects are replicated to extra regions
Standard-IA disables request caching, raising compute charges
rubric: IA lowers storage price but adds retrieval fees, which suit infrequently accessed data.
Other options invent pricing behaviors.

competent.prompt: A reporting-heavy application slows down because many read queries hit the primary RDS instance. The database already uses Multi-AZ. Why won't Multi-AZ help, and what would?
options: Multi-AZ standby is not readable; add a read replica
Multi-AZ standby is readable but needs a larger instance type
Multi-AZ only helps writes; enable Provisioned IOPS only
Multi-AZ replicates asynchronously; switch to a single AZ
rubric: Standard Multi-AZ standby exists for failover and does not serve reads; read replicas scale reads.
Others confuse availability with read scaling.

competent.prompt: An ALB shows all targets as unhealthy though the application runs on the instances. Which could be causes? Select all that apply.
options: The instance security group doesn't allow traffic from the ALB
The health check path returns HTTP 404
The instances lack a public IP address
The app listens on a port different from the health check port
rubric: Blocked traffic, bad path, or wrong port each fail health checks.
A public IP isn't needed as the ALB reaches targets via private IPs.

competent.prompt: Account A owns bucket `data-a` whose bucket policy allows account B's root principal `s3:GetObject`. A role in account B with no S3 permissions in its policies gets AccessDenied reading objects. What is the cause?
options: Bucket policies cannot grant cross-account access
The role also needs an identity policy in account B allowing S3 access
The bucket must be made public for cross-account reads
The role must be recreated in account A
rubric: Cross-account access requires an allow on both the resource side and the caller's identity side.
Others misstate how cross-account trust works.

proficient.prompt: An EC2 instance in a subnet with no public IP cannot reach package repositories. The subnet's route table has `0.0.0.0/0` pointing directly at an internet gateway. What is the most likely cause?
options: The internet gateway only translates addresses for instances that have a public or Elastic IP, so private-only instances need a NAT gateway
The internet gateway cannot route outbound traffic, so the subnet needs a virtual private gateway to reach public sites
The security group is stateful and blocks the return traffic, so an inbound rule for repositories must be added
The route table needs a more specific route for each repository address, since a default route is ignored by gateways
rubric: An internet gateway performs one-to-one NAT only for instances with public IPs, so private-only instances need a NAT gateway.
Distractors misread stateful security groups and the role of virtual private gateways.

proficient.prompt: A role has `s3:GetObject` on a bucket and the bucket policy allows it, yet reads of SSE-KMS encrypted objects fail with AccessDenied. Other unencrypted objects in the bucket read fine. What is the most likely cause?
options: The bucket policy must also name the role's account number in a separate statement for encrypted objects to be readable
The role lacks `kms:Decrypt` permission via the key policy or a grant, so the object cannot be decrypted
S3 blocks all SSE-KMS reads unless the request comes from the same region through a gateway VPC endpoint
The objects' storage class prevents decryption until they are restored by an explicit lifecycle transition
rubric: Reading SSE-KMS objects needs permission to use the KMS key in addition to S3 permissions.
Distractors invent S3-side restrictions rather than checking the KMS layer.

proficient.prompt: A web server's security group allows inbound 443. The subnet's network ACL has inbound allow 443 and outbound allow 443 only, with default deny otherwise. Clients time out. Why?
options: The security group is stateless, so it needs an explicit outbound rule to answer the client requests
The network ACL is stateful, so it blocks the connection until the inbound rule is replicated outbound
The network ACL is stateless, so the outbound rule must allow the ephemeral ports used by client responses
The server needs an Elastic IP, since responses on ephemeral ports are dropped by the internet gateway
rubric: Network ACLs are stateless, so return traffic to the client's ephemeral port needs an outbound allow.
Distractors swap the stateful/stateless behaviour of security groups and network ACLs.

proficient.prompt: A Lambda function attached to private subnets in a VPC times out when calling DynamoDB, but worked before it was attached to the VPC. The subnets have no NAT gateway. What is the best diagnosis?
options: Lambda functions in a VPC lose IAM permissions, so the execution role must be recreated with DynamoDB access
DynamoDB tables only accept connections from the internet, so the function must be moved back to public subnets
The function's memory is too low once attached to a VPC, so the network interface fails to initialise
The subnets have no path to DynamoDB, so a gateway VPC endpoint or NAT route is needed
rubric: Attaching to a VPC removes default internet access; DynamoDB needs a gateway endpoint or NAT path.
Distractors blame IAM, DynamoDB exposure or memory instead of routing.

proficient.prompt: A team enabled RDS Multi-AZ (standard instance deployment) expecting read-heavy dashboards to speed up, but read latency on the primary is unchanged. What explains this?
options: Replication to the standby is synchronous, which adds latency on every read and cancels any gain
The standby exists for failover only and does not serve reads, so read scaling needs read replicas
Multi-AZ only protects storage, so the compute size of the primary must be raised to improve reads
The standby serves reads only after a failover test has been run, which has not yet happened
rubric: The standby in a Multi-AZ instance deployment is for availability and does not serve reads.
Distractors confuse availability with read scaling.

proficient.prompt: A user's identity policy allows `s3:*` on a bucket, yet `PutObject` returns AccessDenied in the same account. Which could explain this? Select all that apply.
options: A permissions boundary on the user that does not include `s3:PutObject`
The identity policy is attached to a group rather than the user, which makes it ignored
An explicit Deny in the bucket policy that matches the user's request
A service control policy in the organization that denies S3 writes
The bucket is in a different region than the user's console session
rubric: Permissions boundaries, explicit denies and SCPs all cap or override identity allows.
Group-attached policies still apply, and console region does not affect S3 authorisation.

proficient.prompt: An Auto Scaling group behind an ALB keeps terminating new instances a minute after launch and replacing them in a loop. The app needs about five minutes to start. The ELB health check is used with a health check grace period of 60 seconds. What is the root cause?
options: The ALB deregistration delay is too long, which causes instances to be removed before they have started
The launch template's AMI is corrupted, so each instance fails its EC2 status checks after boot
The grace period ends before the app is ready, so failed ELB health checks mark instances unhealthy
The scaling policy's cooldown is too short, which forces the group to add instances faster than it needs
rubric: Health checks start counting after the grace period; with a 60s grace and 5 minute startup, instances are replaced prematurely.
Distractors blame deregistration, AMI or cooldown, which don't produce this pattern.

proficient.prompt: Application logs in S3 have unpredictable access: some months nothing is read, others many objects are. The team wants no retrieval fees, no manual lifecycle tuning and low storage cost. Which storage choice best fits?
options: S3 Standard-IA for all objects, because it has lower storage cost and no retrieval charge
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, because it has the lowest storage price and retrieval is typically fast
S3 One Zone-IA for all objects, because it is cheapest and is designed for unpredictable access
S3 Intelligent-Tiering, because it moves objects between tiers automatically with no retrieval fees
rubric: Intelligent-Tiering adapts to unpredictable access without retrieval charges.
Distractors ignore IA retrieval fees or the retrieval delay in Glacier.

proficient.prompt: A production database server runs 24/7 at steady load and must never be interrupted. The commitment is acceptable for three years. Judged on cost and reliability, which purchasing option is best?
options: Spot Instances, because they are the cheapest and the workload can be restarted from backup
On-Demand Instances, because they cost less than commitments when usage is steady and predictable
A Compute or EC2 Instance Savings Plan, because it discounts steady usage without interruption risk
Dedicated Hosts on-demand, because they guarantee no interruptions and are cheaper than any commitment
rubric: Savings Plans or reservations give a large discount for steady usage with no interruption risk.
Spot can be interrupted; On-Demand costs more for steady loads.

proficient.prompt: A CI job in account A must deploy to account B. Criteria: no long-lived secrets, auditable per-session activity, and revocable centrally. Which approach best meets them?
options: Create an IAM user in account B and store its access keys in the CI system's secret store
Create a shared admin IAM user in both accounts and rotate its password every ninety days
Make the deployment bucket public in account B and let the job push artifacts without credentials
Create a role in account B trusting account A's job role, and have the job call `sts:AssumeRole`
rubric: Cross-account roles issue temporary credentials, logged per session, and are revoked by editing the trust or policy.
Distractors rely on long-lived keys, shared users or public access.

proficient.prompt: A web app needs path-based routing to several services, TLS termination and integration with AWS WAF. Traffic is HTTP/HTTPS only. Which load balancer best meets these criteria?
options: Network Load Balancer, because it operates at layer 4 and supports WAF rules on listener ports
Classic Load Balancer, because it supports path routing with a single listener for every service
Application Load Balancer, because it routes on HTTP paths and integrates with AWS WAF
Gateway Load Balancer, because it inspects HTTP paths and terminates TLS for backend services
rubric: ALB works at layer 7 with path rules, TLS termination and WAF integration.
NLB and GWLB don't offer path-based routing or WAF.

proficient.prompt: A service needs RTO of 15 minutes and RPO of seconds after a regional outage, with a budget that rules out full active-active. Which disaster recovery strategy best fits?
options: Backup and restore, because snapshots copied cross-region are cheapest and recover within the RTO
Pilot light with only the database replicated, because compute can always be rebuilt within fifteen minutes
Cold standby with infrastructure code stored, because it has zero running cost and fast deployment
Warm standby with a scaled-down running stack and continuous replication, scaled up on failover
rubric: Warm standby with continuous replication meets a seconds-level RPO and 15-minute RTO below active-active cost.
Backup/restore and cold options typically exceed the RTO; pilot light is slower to scale.

proficient.prompt: A proposal stores a database password in plain text in EC2 launch template user data. Which are valid criticisms? Select all that apply.
options: Anyone with permission to describe the launch template can read the password
The password cannot be rotated without creating a new launch template version
User data is always encrypted at rest with the instance's KMS key, so exposure is impossible
The password is retrievable from the instance metadata service by any process on the instance
User data is limited in size, so a password cannot fit
rubric: User data is readable via API and instance metadata and is hard to rotate, so Secrets Manager or Parameter Store is better.
User data is not automatically encrypted for readers, and size limits don't block a password.

proficient.prompt: A production VPC spans three AZs. A team proposes one NAT gateway in a single AZ to save about two-thirds of NAT cost. Criteria: the app must keep outbound access to external APIs during a single-AZ failure, and cost matters but is secondary. What is the best judgement?
options: Keep one NAT gateway, because it automatically fails over to another AZ when its own AZ fails
Use one NAT gateway per AZ with matching route tables, because it avoids a cross-AZ dependency
Replace NAT with an internet gateway on private subnets, because it removes the single point of failure
Use one NAT instance on a small EC2 size, because it is cheaper and survives AZ failure by default
rubric: A NAT gateway is AZ-scoped; one per AZ keeps outbound access when an AZ fails, satisfying the primary criterion.
Distractors assume automatic cross-AZ failover or misuse IGWs and NAT instances.

novice.prompt: Which AWS service provides resizable virtual servers that you can launch in the cloud?
options: Amazon EC2
Amazon S3
Amazon RDS
Amazon VPC
rubric: EC2 provides virtual servers called instances.
S3 is object storage, RDS is managed databases, VPC is networking; learners confuse these with compute.

novice.prompt: What type of storage is Amazon S3?
options: Object storage
Block storage
Relational database
In-memory cache
rubric: S3 stores data as objects in buckets.
Block storage describes EBS, a common confusion.

novice.prompt: What does IAM stand for in AWS?
options: Identity and Access Management
Instance and Application Manager
Internal Access Monitor
Integrated Account Metrics
rubric: IAM is Identity and Access Management, used to control who can do what.
Other options are plausible-sounding invented expansions.

novice.prompt: Which AWS service is a managed relational database service supporting engines such as MySQL and PostgreSQL?
options: Amazon RDS
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon S3
Amazon Route 53
rubric: RDS is the managed relational database service.
DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value service, often confused with RDS.

options: A separate geographic area containing multiple Availability Zones
A single data center building
A type of EC2 instance
A billing account group
rubric: A Region is a geographic area with multiple AZs.
Learners often equate a Region or AZ with a single data center.

novice.prompt: Which of the following are AWS database services? Select all that apply.
options: Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon Aurora
Amazon CloudFront
Amazon EBS
rubric: DynamoDB and Aurora are database services.
CloudFront is a CDN and EBS is block storage.

novice.prompt: A new team member must create a private network section in AWS where their servers will run, with their own IP address range and subnets. Which AWS service is used to define this virtual network?
options: Amazon VPC
Amazon CloudWatch
AWS Lambda
Amazon SNS
rubric: VPC lets you define an isolated virtual network with subnets.
CloudWatch is monitoring; Lambda is serverless compute; SNS is messaging.

novice.prompt: Why would you store a website's images in S3 instead of on an EC2 instance's local disk?
options: S3 keeps data durably and independently of any single server
S3 objects are faster to edit in place like a disk
S3 is required for any EC2 instance to boot
S3 files are automatically free of charge
rubric: S3 offers durable storage separate from instance lifecycle.
Distractors assume S3 behaves like a disk, is mandatory, or is free.

novice.prompt: What does it mean that an IAM policy follows the principle of least privilege?
options: Users get only the permissions needed for their tasks
Users get all permissions and lose some later
Only the root user may have any permissions
Permissions are removed after one day
rubric: Least privilege grants the minimum permissions required.
Other options misread it as default-open, root-only or time-limited.

novice.prompt: Why do architects deploy an application across two Availability Zones?
options: So it keeps running if one zone has a failure
So it runs twice as fast on every request
So data is stored in two countries automatically
So the bill is cut in half by sharing
rubric: Multiple AZs provide fault tolerance.
Learners mistake AZs for performance, country distribution or cost savings.

novice.prompt: What is the main difference between a public subnet and a private subnet in a VPC?
options: A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway; a private one does not
A public subnet is free; a private subnet is billed
A public subnet is in another Region from a private one
A public subnet holds databases; a private one holds servers
rubric: Public subnets route to an internet gateway.
Distractors invent cost, region or role differences.

novice.prompt: Which statement best explains how EC2 pricing with On-Demand instances works?
options: You pay for the compute time you use without long-term commitment
You pay a fixed yearly fee regardless of usage
You pay only when the instance is idle and stopped
You pay once and own the physical server
rubric: On-Demand is pay-as-you-go.
Distractors describe reservations, inverted billing or ownership.

novice.prompt: Which statements correctly describe IAM roles? Select all that apply.
options: They provide temporary credentials to a service or user that assumes them
They let an EC2 instance access S3 without stored access keys
They must be tied to one person's password
They are the same thing as the root account
rubric: Roles give temporary credentials, avoiding hard-coded keys.
Roles are not passwords or the root account.

novice.prompt: A developer stores an access key in a file on an EC2 instance so the app can read an S3 bucket. A colleague suggests attaching an IAM role to the instance instead. Why is the role the better choice?
options: It supplies temporary credentials automatically, so no long-lived key sits on the disk
It makes the S3 bucket public so no credentials are needed
It encrypts the instance's disk without any extra setup
It gives the app the same rights as the root user
rubric: Roles avoid storing long-lived secrets.
Distractors misstate roles as making buckets public, encrypting disks, or granting root.

expert.prompt: A teammate says a role in account A can read objects in an S3 bucket in account B once the role's identity policy allows s3:GetObject on that bucket's ARN. Which critique is correct?
options: Wrong: the identity policy alone is enough, because the role is already authenticated inside AWS and the bucket owner has no say
Wrong: the bucket policy in account B must also allow the role, because cross-account access needs an allow on both sides
Wrong: only the bucket policy matters, so the role needs no S3 permissions in account A because the bucket owner decides
Wrong: cross-account reads need an S3 ACL on every object, because bucket and identity policies cannot grant across accounts
rubric: Cross-account access requires an allow in the caller's identity policy and in the resource policy of the other account.
Distractors assume one side suffices or that only ACLs work across accounts.

expert.prompt: Private-subnet workers pull about 40 TB a month from S3 in the same Region through a NAT gateway. Criteria: cut cost, keep traffic off the public internet, make no code changes. Which option is best?
options: Add an S3 gateway endpoint and route-table entry, removing NAT data-processing charges for that S3 traffic
Add a second NAT gateway in each AZ, since spreading the traffic lowers the per-GB processing charge
Move workers to public subnets with Elastic IPs, since that avoids NAT charges and still stays private
Replace NAT with an S3 interface endpoint, since gateway endpoints are billed per GB in the same way as NAT
rubric: S3 gateway endpoints have no hourly or per-GB charge and keep traffic on the AWS network.
Distractors misread NAT pricing, or use public subnets, which sends traffic through the internet gateway.

expert.prompt: In a design review someone says: 'An RDS read replica in another AZ gives us automatic failover with zero data loss, so we can skip Multi-AZ.' Which evaluation is right?
options: Right: replicas replicate synchronously, and RDS promotes them automatically whenever the primary instance fails
Wrong: replicas must sit in the primary's AZ, so they cannot provide any resilience against an AZ outage
Wrong: replication is asynchronous and replicas are not automatic failover targets, so Multi-AZ better meets zero-loss failover
Right: replicas share the primary's storage volume, so no committed writes can be lost when failing over
rubric: Read replicas are asynchronous and need manual promotion; a Multi-AZ standby is synchronous with automatic failover.
Distractors confuse replicas with Multi-AZ standbys or invent shared storage.

expert.prompt: Steady compute of about $20 per hour runs 24/7 for the next year. During the year the team will move some services from EC2 to Fargate and change instance families. Criterion: maximise discount while keeping that flexibility. Which is best?
options: Standard Reserved Instances for the current instance family, since they give the deepest EC2-only discount
A one-year Compute Savings Plan, since the hourly commitment applies across EC2, Fargate and Lambda usage
Spot Instances for every service, since Spot is cheapest and the workload happens to run continuously
On-Demand pricing with no commitment, since any commitment would block changing services during the year
rubric: Compute Savings Plans discount usage across instance families and services such as Fargate.
Standard RIs lock the instance family; Spot suits interruptible work, not a steady baseline.

expert.prompt: Objects of several MB have unpredictable access patterns. Requirements: millisecond retrieval, no retrieval fees, and lowest storage cost without manual analysis. Which S3 storage class is best?
options: S3 Standard-IA, since its infrequent-access pricing is lower and retrieval stays immediate
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, since archive classes always give the lowest cost per GB stored
S3 Intelligent-Tiering, since it moves objects between access tiers automatically without retrieval fees
S3 One Zone-IA, since using one zone is cheaper and retrieval fees do not apply to that class
rubric: Intelligent-Tiering adapts to unpredictable access with no retrieval charges and millisecond access.
Standard-IA and One Zone-IA charge retrieval fees; Glacier Flexible Retrieval is not millisecond.

expert.prompt: A design runs an Auto Scaling group across two AZs in private subnets, with one NAT gateway in AZ-a, IAM user AdministratorAccess keys stored in a file on each instance, and RDS Multi-AZ. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.
options: The keys are long-lived and over-privileged; an instance role with least-privilege permissions would be safer
The single NAT gateway makes AZ-a a dependency for outbound traffic from instances in both AZs
RDS Multi-AZ is redundant because the Auto Scaling group already protects the database tier from failure
Instances in private subnets cannot receive patches, so they should be moved into public subnets
rubric: Static admin keys violate least privilege and role-based credentials; one NAT is an AZ-level single point of failure.
Auto Scaling does not protect stateful databases, and private instances can be patched via NAT or endpoints.

expert.prompt: A nightly job runs about 5 hours, is CPU-heavy, and writes checkpoints to S3 every 5 minutes so it can resume after interruption. Finance wants the lowest cost, and the job has a 10-hour window. Which compute choice best fits?
options: Lambda functions chained by Step Functions, since Lambda removes idle cost for any single long-running task
An always-on On-Demand EC2 fleet sized for peak, since uninterrupted capacity is required for long jobs
AWS Batch on EC2 Spot capacity, resuming from checkpoints after interruptions, since the window allows retries
Fargate On-Demand tasks, since they avoid instance management and are cheaper than Spot for long jobs
rubric: Checkpointed, deadline-tolerant work suits Spot, which is the cheapest capacity.
Distractors ignore the 15-minute Lambda limit, pay for idle fleets, or assume On-Demand beats Spot.

expert.prompt: CloudTrail logs from all accounts must be tamper-resistant even against administrators of the source accounts, and retained for 7 years. Which design meets this?
options: An account trail to a bucket in the same account, with versioning and MFA delete enabled for 7 years
An organization trail to a bucket in a separate log-archive account with Object Lock in compliance mode for 7 years
An organization trail to a log-archive bucket with a lifecycle rule moving objects to Glacier after one day
Trails in each account writing to CloudWatch Logs with 7-year retention and access limited to administrators
rubric: A separate account plus Object Lock compliance mode prevents deletion or alteration even by privileged users.
Same-account, lifecycle-only or log-group designs can still be changed by administrators.

expert.prompt: A Lambda function in a VPC must reach an RDS MySQL database. Requirements: no database password in code or environment variables, and surviving bursts of 1,000 concurrent invocations without exhausting connections. Which design meets both?
options: Connect directly, reading the password from Secrets Manager on each invocation and opening a new connection
Connect through RDS Proxy using IAM database authentication, with the Lambda role allowed rds-db:connect
Connect directly with a KMS-encrypted password in an environment variable and a raised max_connections setting
Run Lambda outside the VPC and use a public RDS endpoint with a password stored in Parameter Store
rubric: RDS Proxy pools connections and IAM authentication removes the stored password from the function.
Other options keep passwords in the function path or leave connection exhaustion unsolved.

expert.prompt: A game needs players in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 to write locally with low latency, tolerate a full Region loss, and see replication lag of about a second. Which data layer meets all of these?
options: Aurora Global Database with the writer in us-east-1 and a read-only secondary cluster in eu-west-1
DynamoDB global tables with replicas in both Regions, and clients using their local Region's endpoint
DynamoDB with AWS Backup copying snapshots to eu-west-1 hourly and restoring after a Region loss
RDS Multi-AZ in us-east-1 with a cross-Region read replica in eu-west-1 promoted manually on failure
rubric: Global tables give multi-Region active-active writes with replication typically within about a second.
Aurora Global has a single writer; backup copies and replicas give far worse RPO and no local writes.

expert.prompt: A vendor's AWS account must read only the `exports/` prefix of your bucket. Requirements: no long-lived keys, and protection against the vendor's other customers tricking the vendor into using your role. Which design meets this?
options: An IAM user for the vendor with access keys scoped to the prefix, rotated every 90 days
A role trusting any principal, protected only by a unique ExternalId and a policy limited to the prefix
A role trusting the vendor's account with a unique ExternalId condition and permissions limited to the prefix
A public-read bucket policy on the prefix, with an unguessable object-key naming scheme to deter outsiders
rubric: A role trusted by the vendor account with ExternalId avoids long-lived keys and mitigates the confused deputy problem.
Other options use static keys, trust anyone, or rely on obscurity.

expert.prompt: Instances in private subnets with no internet route must use SQS and S3, and only principals from your AWS Organization may use these paths. Which design meets this?
options: A NAT gateway with security groups that allow only the published AWS public IP ranges for SQS and S3
An interface endpoint for SQS and a gateway endpoint for S3, with endpoint policies on aws:PrincipalOrgID
Gateway endpoints for both SQS and S3, with a network ACL limiting traffic to the organization's accounts
An internet gateway and public IPs on the instances, with IAM policies restricting the queue and the bucket
rubric: SQS uses an interface endpoint and S3 a gateway endpoint; endpoint policies can restrict by organization ID.
SQS has no gateway endpoint, NACLs cannot filter by account, and NAT or public IPs break the no-internet requirement.

expert.prompt: You must serve a static site worldwide at https://www.example.com from a private S3 bucket. Which components belong in a design that meets this? Select all that apply.
options: A CloudFront distribution using origin access control, with a bucket policy allowing only that distribution
An ACM certificate requested in us-east-1 and attached to the distribution
A Route 53 alias record for www pointing to the distribution
The bucket made public with a website endpoint, so CloudFront can fetch objects without extra policies
An ACM certificate requested in the bucket's Region, since CloudFront reads certificates from the origin's Region
rubric: OAC keeps the bucket private, CloudFront certificates must be in us-east-1, and an alias record maps the domain.
Public buckets break the private requirement, and the origin Region is irrelevant for CloudFront certificates.

expert.prompt: An order pipeline sends messages to an SQS standard queue consumed by Lambda. Malformed messages are retried until the 4-day retention expires, then vanish unseen, while using up consumer capacity. Requirements: no message silently lost, and poison messages set aside for inspection. What is the design missing?
options: A dead-letter queue with a redrive policy and maxReceiveCount, plus an alarm on its depth
A longer retention period of 14 days, so that failing messages have more time to eventually succeed
A switch to a FIFO queue, since FIFO queues automatically discard messages that cannot be processed
A visibility timeout of zero, so that failed messages return at once and are retried much faster
rubric: A DLQ isolates messages after repeated failures so they can be inspected rather than expiring silently.
Longer retention, FIFO, or zero visibility timeout do not isolate poison messages and may worsen the problem.
